ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee at the Faculty of Medicine at LMU Munich (reference number: 23-0268) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2013).
All autistic participants had a confirmed diagnosis of either F84.5, F84.0, or F84.1 according to ICD-10(34), without comorbid neurological conditions.
They were recruited from the autism outpatient clinic database at the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, LMU Munich, and through local autism network contacts.
We recruited a total of 71 individuals, comprising 32 autistic participants and 39 TD participants.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, as assessed with the Landolt ring eye vision test (37) and the Ishihara test for color blindness (38).

table.text: Participants had to identify the orientation of a line segment within a diamond target presented among five non-diamond distractors.
Before each session, participants completed ten practice trials to familiarize themselves with task requirements and response mappings, with opportunities for clarification questions.
Participants had to identify the diamond target and determine its internal line orientation as quickly and accurately as possible.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Power analysis using PANGEA v0.2(35) determined our target sample size based on the effect size (d = 0.33) reported in Allenmark et al. (28). To achieve 90% power with an alpha level of 0.05, a sample size of 24 participants per group would be required to detect the critical interaction between group and distractor prevalence. We recruited a total of 71 individuals, comprising 32 autistic participants and 39 TD participants. Data from eight TD participants was excluded either due to incomplete eye-tracking data or elevated scores on the Ritvo Autism Diagnostic Scale -Revised (RADS-R)(36) indicating autism-like traits. Data from four autistic participants was also omitted due to incomplete or poor-quality eye-tracking data.

live_data_statements: All autistic participants had a confirmed diagnosis of either F84.5, F84.0, or F84.1 according to ICD-10(34), without comorbid neurological conditions.
They were recruited from the autism outpatient clinic database at the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, LMU Munich, and through local autism network contacts.
We recruited a total of 71 individuals, comprising 32 autistic participants and 39 TD participants.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, as assessed with the Landolt ring eye vision test (37) and the Ishihara test for color blindness (38).
Participants had to identify the orientation of a line segment within a diamond target presented among five non-diamond distractors.
Before each session, participants completed ten practice trials to familiarize themselves with task requirements and response mappings, with opportunities for clarification questions.
Participants had to identify the diamond target and determine its internal line orientation as quickly and accurately as possible.

Interestingly, this distractor interference was larger for autistic participants than TD participants (Group × Singleton), F(1, 57) = 13.86, p < .001, ηp² = .196, indicating that autistic participants were more affected by the presence of distractors.
Autistic participants were more likely to avoid looking towards the cued direction under high-prevalence conditions when no salient distractor appeared there.
We would also like to thank our participants for their support and participation in our research.

text.text: Background: Within predictive coding accounts of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), two competing explanations locate perceptual atypicalities within inference: weak prior formation versus altered weighting of prediction errors.

We propose the atypical iterative prior updating (AIPU) account, which shifts the locus from inference to what happens afterwards: sensory evidence is overweighted during iterative belief updating over time.
The accounts predict distinct temporal signatures of attentional divergence.

Methods: To distinguish among the accounts, we presented autistic and typically developing adults with a distractor suppression paradigm using a 100%-valid spatial cue and varying distractor prevalence, while eye movements tracked the temporal dynamics of attentional selection.
Results: Both groups showed equivalent first-fixation capture, ruling out prior-formation differences.
Distractor prevalence modulated interference differently across groups.
Autistic participants produced larger reaction time interference, more fixations, and more target refixations, a pattern emerging after initial selection.
These findings locate ASD-related differences specifically in iterative updating across time, not in perceptual inference.

Conclusions: The mechanism points to sustained attentional engagement: rather than terminating sensory sampling once expectations are confirmed, autistic individuals continue accumulating evidence even under perfect predictability.
The world might feel "too much" not because perceptual inference is altered, but because updating continues beyond resolution.
Visual search in everyday life requires not only finding what is relevant but continuously suppressing what is salient yet irrelevant.

Many autistic individuals describe environments that feel noisy and difficult to filter(1-4), whereas experimental studies report typical or even superior performance on certain perceptual tasks (5) (6) (7) (8).

text.text: This discrepancy fuels a debate about attentional control in autism spectrum disorder (ASD): Do salient events capture attention more strongly in ASD, or do differences emerge after attention is engaged?
Two frameworks address this discrepancy.
Classic attentional accounts emphasize competition between stimulus-driven salience (9) (10) (11) (12) and goal-driven control (13) (14) (15) (16) (17) (18) (19).

text.text: Predictive coding accounts frame perception as inference under uncertainty, combining prior expectations with sensory evidence weighted by their precision (24) (25) (26).
text.formatted: Predictive coding accounts frame perception as inference under uncertainty, combining prior expectations with sensory evidence weighted by their precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, differences in ASD reflect atypical estimation or use of precision: overweighting immediate sensory input while underweighting priors during perceptual inference (27), or atypical weighting of prediction errors (24, 26), particularly for surprising events (28).
text.formatted: Within this framework, differences in ASD reflect atypical estimation or use of precision: overweighting immediate sensory input while underweighting priors during perceptual inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref>, or atypical weighting of prediction errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26)</ref>, particularly for surprising events <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>.

text.text: When sensory input violates expectations, autistic individuals may treat the mismatch as highly informative evidence demanding high weight rather than noise to discount.

Recent work points to a different locus: Shi et al. (29) showed that autistic individuals integrate prior knowledge typically for immediate perceptual estimates, contradicting the weak-prior account (27).
text.formatted: Recent work points to a different locus: Shi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> showed that autistic individuals integrate prior knowledge typically for immediate perceptual estimates, contradicting the weak-prior account <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref>.

text.text: We term this perspective atypical iterative prior updating (AIPU).

Unlike precision-regulation accounts, AIPU specifies that sensory evidence is overweighted not during perceptual inference (i.e. prior + likelihood → posterior), but during the updating of priors over time (i.e. posteriorₜ → priorₜ₊₁).
Evidence from perceptual estimation (28, 29) and learning paradigms (30) supports the AIPU account.
text.formatted: Evidence from perceptual estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29)</ref> and learning paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref> supports the AIPU account.

text.text: Whether AIPU extends to attentional control remains unclear.
Some studies point to increased distraction by salient but irrelevant stimuli in ASD, consistent with stronger bottom-up capture or weaker top-down suppression (31, 32).
text.formatted: Some studies point to increased distraction by salient but irrelevant stimuli in ASD, consistent with stronger bottom-up capture or weaker top-down suppression <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32)</ref>.

text.text: Other studies find intact or even advantageous performance, particularly when regularities allow the construction of reliable priors (28).
text.formatted: Other studies find intact or even advantageous performance, particularly when regularities allow the construction of reliable priors <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>.

text.text: Allenmark et al. (28) provided critical evidence showing that both ASD and typically developing (TD) groups acquired spatial priors equally, deploying them to guide where to look (the pre-selective stage) with comparable effectiveness.
text.formatted: Allenmark et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> provided critical evidence showing that both ASD and typically developing (TD) groups acquired spatial priors equally, deploying them to guide where to look (the pre-selective stage) with comparable effectiveness.

text.text: Crucially, differences emerged at the post-selective stage: when a target appeared at the location previously occupied by a rare-region distractor, the ASD group showed a coincidence effect, reflected in prolonged processing and re-checking, five times larger than that shown by the TD group.

These findings localize the core difference in ASD not at initial attentional capture, but in what happens after a salient event is encountered: the speed of disengagement from irrelevant information and the translation of perceptual evidence into decisions.

Both AIPU (29) and precision-regulation accounts (24, 26, 28) agree on a common principle: autistic individuals process prediction errors differently, not because they fail to form priors, but because they weigh unexpected sensory evidence more heavily.
text.formatted: Both AIPU <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> and precision-regulation accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28)</ref> agree on a common principle: autistic individuals process prediction errors differently, not because they fail to form priors, but because they weigh unexpected sensory evidence more heavily.

text.text: The accounts diverge on when: precision-regulation places the overweighting within perceptual inference; AIPU specifies it in the iterative updating of beliefs across time.
This divergence generates testable predictions for attentional control.
First, Allenmark et al. (28) showed intact acquisition of statistical regularities but heightened sensitivity to surprising deviations from them.
text.formatted: First, Allenmark et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> showed intact acquisition of statistical regularities but heightened sensitivity to surprising deviations from them.

text.text: Does this dissociation between "where to look" and "what is there" depend on learning spatial priors from statistical regularities, or does it persist even when priors are provided explicitly, trial-by-trial, via perfectly valid spatial cues?
If the difference lies in a weak priority itself or deploying priors, perfect cues should substantially reduce or eliminate group differences.
In contrast, if it reflects more dynamic, sensory-driven belief updating, as Shi et al. (29) demonstrated, then even a 100%-valid cue may not fully shield against distractor interference.
text.formatted: In contrast, if it reflects more dynamic, sensory-driven belief updating, as Shi et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> demonstrated, then even a 100%-valid cue may not fully shield against distractor interference.

text.text: Second, if the core difference lies in iterative updating rather than prior itself, it should surface not only in manual response times but also in the temporal unfolding of attention.
Autistic individuals should exhibit more total fixations (deeper search) and more frequent returns to the target to confirm identity before committing to a response.
Such temporal signatures would directly reflect sustained sensory engagement that prolongs processing, present even when distractors are frequent and thus less surprising.

The present study tests these alternatives by pairing a 100%-valid spatial cue, signaling exactly where a distractor will appear, with session-wise manipulation of distractor prevalence (low vs. high), which varies how often distractors occur and thus how expected they are.
Because prevalence determines the balance between prior expectations and sensory evidence, group differences in how prevalence modulates distractor interference directly index perceptual inference.
In TD individuals, explicit spatial cues allow proactive suppression, reducing oculomotor capture (33).
text.formatted: In TD individuals, explicit spatial cues allow proactive suppression, reducing oculomotor capture <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(33)</ref>.

text.text: Three predictions follow.

If the core difference in ASD reflects weak spatial prior or deployment, both groups should benefit from the 100%-valid cue, but the ASD group should still show more initial oculomotor capture by distractors.
General precision-regulation accounts predict that group differences should emerge in perceptual inference, reflecting differences in the adaptive, context-dependent weighting of prediction errors.

The AIPU account predicts neither differences in initial capture nor in prevalence modulation, but prolonged post-selective processing: more total fixations across the trial (deeper search), and more returns to the target location (sustained engagement with sensory evidence).
Eye-movement recording pinpoints the temporal stage at which these alternatives diverge.

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee at the Faculty of Medicine at LMU Munich (reference number: 23-0268) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2013).
All participants submitted a written declaration of consent prior to experiment commencement and received monetary compensation for their participation in the complete study.
All autistic participants had a confirmed diagnosis of either F84.5, F84.0, or F84.1 according to ICD-10(34), without comorbid neurological conditions.
They were recruited from the autism outpatient clinic database at the Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, LMU Munich, and through local autism network contacts.
TD participants reported no neurological or psychiatric conditions and confirmed no use of psychotropic medication.
Power analysis using PANGEA v0.2(35) determined our target sample size based on the effect size (d = 0.33) reported in Allenmark et al. (28).
text.formatted: Power analysis using PANGEA v0.2(35) determined our target sample size based on the effect size (d = 0.33) reported in Allenmark et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>.

text.text: To achieve 90% power with an alpha level of 0.05, a sample size of 24 participants per group would be required to detect the critical interaction between group and distractor prevalence.
We recruited a total of 71 individuals, comprising 32 autistic participants and 39 TD participants.
Data from eight TD participants was excluded either due to incomplete eye-tracking data or elevated scores on the Ritvo Autism Diagnostic Scale -Revised (RADS-R)(36) indicating autism-like traits.
Data from four autistic participants was also omitted due to incomplete or poor-quality eye-tracking data.

The final analyzed sample comprised 28 autistic adults (age range: 20-44 years, M = 29.8, SD = 7.1; 16 males, 12 females) and 31 TD adults (age range: 19-41 years, M = 28.4, SD = 5.6; 14 males, 17 females).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, as assessed with the Landolt ring eye vision test (37) and the Ishihara test for color blindness (38).

text.text: The two groups were similar in terms of age, vision and color blindness scores, IQ scores as measured by the Culture Fair Test (CFT-20-R) (39), as well as concentration and speed (d2 test of attention)(40) (Table 1).

We did, however, use the scores from BDI, IU, and STAI trait measures for additional correlation analyses to reveal any individual differences in distractor interference (see Supplementary Information).
Testing occurred in a well-lit experimental cabin featuring sealed doors to minimize auditory interference.
Participants sat 57 cm away from a Dell UltraSharp U2412M LCD Monitor
We employed a statistical learning paradigm to examine distractor suppression under two distractor prevalence conditions.
Participants had to identify the orientation of a line segment within a diamond target presented among five non-diamond distractors.
A singleton color distractor (either orange among cyan items or cyan among orange items) appeared on certain trials; its color was randomized across trials.
The experimental manipulation centered on distractor prevalence, implemented across two counterbalanced sessions.
One session featured low distractor prevalence (50% singleton presence), while the other featured high distractor prevalence (90% singleton presence).
Session order was counterbalanced across participants both between and within groups to control for potential order effects.
Cue-distractor validity remained at 100% throughout all conditions, with the line cue reliably pointing to the singleton distractor location when present and to a random location when absent.
Each session comprised 10 blocks of 20 trials each, yielding 400 trials per participant across both sessions.
This structure provided sufficient statistical power for detecting prevalence-dependent learning effects while maintaining manageable block durations for sustained attention.
Before each session, participants completed ten practice trials to familiarize themselves with task requirements and response mappings, with opportunities for clarification questions.

PsychoPy software controlled experimental presentation, with session-specific parameters (participant identification, session number, distractor prevalence, cue validity) configured via a dialog interface.
Eye-tracker calibration employed a standard five-point procedure, followed by validation.
Instruction screens were then displayed explaining the task.
Each trial began with a fixation cross lasting 500 ms.
A white line cue subsequently appeared alongside the fixation cross, forming the cue display (500 ms).
Participants received instructions to ignore the line cue and maintain focus on the fixation cross.
The search display then appeared and remained visible until response execution via keyboard input.
The inter-trial interval was jittered between 1.0-1.5 s.
Participants had to identify the diamond target and determine its internal line orientation as quickly and accurately as possible.
Horizontal line orientations required left arrow key responses, while vertical orientations required up arrow key responses.
Instructions emphasized ignoring any color distractors appearing in the search display.
After each block, an accuracy report appeared, encouraging participants to maintain optimal performance levels.
Following the first session, participants could take a short break and complete questionnaires.
After the break, eye-tracker recalibration was performed before the second session proceeded with identical procedures but adjusted distractor prevalence settings.
We excluded outlier trials when response times (RTs) fell below 0.1s or exceeded individual participant means by three standard deviations in either direction, or when responses were incorrect.
This preprocessing eliminated 1.33% of trials, which was relatively low.
All subsequent analyses examined correct trials only.
Primary RT analysis employed a mixed ANOVA examining response latencies across experimental conditions.
This analysis incorporated RT as the dependent variable, Singleton Presence (absent/present) and Distractor Prevalence as the within-subject factors, and Group (ASD/TD) as the between-subject factor.

Distractor interference analysis quantified the cognitive cost imposed by the presence of singletons through a derived measure calculated as the difference between RTs for singletons present and absent for each participant and prevalence condition.
A similar mixed ANOVA was employed to examine this interference.
Eye-movement data underwent analysis using 1.5° visual angle regions of interest positioned around each stimulus location.
Fixation measures included target and distractor fixation frequencies, fixation durations, and the first fixations, providing insight into attentional allocation patterns during visual search.
Separate mixed ANOVAs were used to capture within-group and between-group attentional dynamics.

Autistic participants were more likely to avoid looking towards the cued direction under high-prevalence conditions when no salient distractor appeared there.

To explore whether attentional control differences relate to self-reported intolerance of uncertainty (IU), we correlated each participant's mean distractor interference (averaged across prevalence) with their IU score (for more details, see Supplementary Information).
The overall correlation was significant, p = .0015.

However, after partialling out Group, the correlation was no longer significant, p = .64, indicating that the association was largely driven by between-group differences rather than a continuous within-group relationship.
In short, behaviorally, autistic participants showed pronounced distractor interference despite perfect cue validity, whereas TD participants showed minimal or no interference.

Eye movements suggest similar initial capture by singleton distractors across groups, but autistic participants exhibited more total fixations and more target refixations-consistent with sustained engagement with sensory information and deeper search.

Predictive processing differences in ASD manifested neither in initial attentional capture, indicating intact deployment of spatial priors, nor in how distractor interference was modulated by prevalence, indicating preserved perceptual inference.

Instead, group differences emerged at later processing stages: autistic participants showed increased response times, more fixations, and more frequent target refixations, consistent with the AIPU account's prediction that differences arise in the temporal dynamics of belief updating following salient events.
Specifically, the first-fixation results argue against a capture account.
Both groups were drawn to the singleton distractor equally, replicating previous reports of intact initial orienting in ASD and high-autistictrait samples (28, 45).

text.text: Phasic precision accounts specifically predict that atypical processing should scale with surprise, strongest for unexpected events and diminishing as events become predictable (28).

text.text: The current data do not conform to this prediction: autistic participants showed interference even in the high-prevalence condition, where distractors were highly expected.
The larger interference effects found in ASD might appear to indicate altered perceptual inference.

However, eye-tracking localized group differences to post-selective processing stages, suggesting that the elevated interference across prevalence levels observed in ASD arguably arises from prolonged iterative updating rather than atypical perceptual inference.
Together, these findings argue against accounts that attribute predictive processing differences in ASD to altered, contextdependent weighting of prediction errors during perceptual inference.
Autistic participants made more fixations overall, particularly when singleton distractors were present, and returned to targets more frequently compared to TD participants.

Critically, while both groups showed fixation-based interference under low prevalence, only the ASD group showed interference under high prevalence conditions, where distractors were highly expected, though the Group × Prevalence interaction did not reach significance.

Under high prevalence, autistic participants made fewer fixations on the cued distractor location when no singleton distractor appeared there, demonstrating that the ASD group learned the prevalence statistics (frequency prior) to avoid the cued location.

This pattern rules out a simple failure of proactive suppression (which would predict more distractor refixations and a stronger prevalence benefit) and instead points to sustained post-selective processing difference in ASD.

These results support the AIPU account (29), and suggest a mechanistic process: sustained attentional engagement reflects the accumulation of sensory information for iterative updating of priors over time (i.e. posterior-to-prior updating).

text.text: When a singleton distractor appears , the system must update its belief about what is present at that location.
Under AIPU, this updating process requires continued visual sampling before the belief stabilizes.

Increased target refixations reflect re-checking to accumulate confirmatory evidence, while the overall increase in fixations signals deeper search to resolve conflict between prior expectation and current sensory evidence.
This interpretation aligns with formal accounts of decision-making.
Findings from drift-diffusion models support the view that evidence accumulation thresholds, not perceptual sensitivity, differ in ASD (46).
text.formatted: Findings from drift-diffusion models support the view that evidence accumulation thresholds, not perceptual sensitivity, differ in ASD <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(46)</ref>.

text.text: The overweighting of sensory evidence in iterative updating, as suggested by the AIPU account, would map to larger effective evidence thresholds, requiring more fixations and more target re-checking before response commitment.
Future computational modelling studies will be required to test this suggestion.
The correlation between intolerance of uncertainty and distractor interference was significant but became non-significant after controlling for Group.

Rather than IU driving atypical attentional control, the AIPU account suggests the reverse: the iterative updating mechanism gives each sensory sample excessive weight, generating persistent residual uncertainty that may give rise to heightened experience of uncertainty in ASD.
In this view, the habitual experience of a less stable perceptual world could foster avoidance of uncertain situations, manifesting as elevated trait IU.
The cross-sectional nature of our data precludes directional inference, but future longitudinal or computational work could test this prediction.
Our sample size was adequate for the observed effects (df ≈ 57), but the perfectly valid cue and simple visual search display limit ecological validity.
Whether our findings generalize to more naturalistic, complex scenes with higher target-distractor similarity and more ambiguous priors remains to be tested.
We also cannot rule out that a larger sample might detect surprise-grading, given that descriptive means show some numerical variation across prevalences in ASD (RT interference: Low = 52.9 ms vs.
High = 72.9 ms).

Furthermore, given the high comorbidity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in ASD, future studies should test this paradigm in an ADHD sample to disentangle ADHD-related attentional difficulties from AIPU-related updating.
Additionally, varying cue validity, salience, or error costs may reveal conditions under which distractor prevalence exerts greater influence.

In conclusion, the present study reframes predictive processing differences in ASD: the issue is not whether priors are weak or prediction errors are amplified, but how long updating persists once a salient event occurs.

A clear processing stage-specific pattern emerges: spatial priors are formed and deployed effectively, and perceptual inference is largely preserved; yet differences emerge during post-selective processing.

Autistic participants continued sampling sensory evidence even when distractor occurrence was highly expected, in line with the AIPU account(29) rather than strictly phasic precision-regulation accounts (28).

text.text: Across paradigms, spanning spatial prior learning (28), probabilistic associative learning of facial emotion recognition(30), temporal estimation(47), and attentional control in the present study, a converging pattern emerges: sustained sensory engagement constitutes a unifying mechanism through which atypical iterative prior updating unfolds.

The fixation cross (Figure 1) consists of a grey circle background (0.5° diameter), a black cross (0.5°×0.5°), and a central grey dot (0.1° diameter), while the cue display consists of a white line cue (2°×0.5°) alongside the fixation.
The line direction indicated the potential location of an upcoming singleton distractor with perfect validity when such distractors appeared.

The search display presented six colored items against a black background: one diamond target (3°×3°) and five distractor shapes randomly selected from circles (3° diameter), triangles (3.06°×3.06°), pentagons (3°×3°), and hexagons (3°×3°).
Only the diamond target contained a horizontal or vertical line segment, while all distractors featured oblique lines (0.3°×1.5°).

Items appeared at six equidistant locations positioned 6° of visual angle from the display center, with random assignment ensuring equal probability of target and distractor appearance at each location.
On some trials, a singleton distractor differed in color (cyan/orange) from other items; target and singleton distractor colors alternated randomly across trials.
For example, when the diamond target and standard distractors appeared in cyan, the singleton distractor would appear in orange.
Trials without a singleton distractor presented all items in uniform coloration-either entirely cyan or entirely orange.

The fixation display consisting of a fixation cross was shown for 500 ms, followed by the appearance of a line cue for a further 500 ms.
The visual search display then appeared with the search target being the diamond shape, and the singleton distractor being the object with a unique color (here the orange item).
Participants responded to the orientation of the line segment inside the target diamond shape (here horizontal).
